title: We thank you
hook: everyone bows at "we give thanks"; the rabbis say this blessing is said by all
carry: no one can say it for you

segments.voice: Yesterday, shome'a tefillah, the blank space in the Amidah. Your line was your own words here. Did you write your private request down? Today, the asking is over, and the thanks begins. Day five hundred ninety-three.

When the leader repeats the Amidah out loud, the congregation mostly listens. They answer amen at the end of each blessing, and let the leader speak for them. You can ask on someone's behalf. You can be represented. Then the leader reaches one blessing, bows, and the whole room does something different. Everyone starts murmuring their own words, at the same time, quietly, as if to say: no, this one, I'll do myself.
screen: `THE ROOM LISTENS AND ANSWERS AMEN.` → `ONE BLESSING, EVERYONE BOWS.` → `THIS ONE, I'LL DO MYSELF.`

segments.voice: After a short blessing asking that prayer be accepted, called Retzeh, comes the eighteenth: Modim. It begins: we thank You, for You are the Lord our God and the God of our ancestors forever. Then it lists: for our lives, entrusted to Your hand. For our souls, in Your keeping. For Your miracles that are with us every day, and Your wonders and goodness at every time: evening, morning and noon. Not the parting of the sea. The miracles of every day. People bow at its first word and at its end, as they did at the start of the Amidah. And when the leader repeats it aloud, the congregation says its own quiet version, called Modim d'Rabbanan, the Modim of the rabbis. The Talmud, in Sotah 40a, collects the different words several rabbis said here, and later commentators explain why everyone joins in: someone else can make a request for you, but no one can say thank you on your behalf. The word itself, modim, can mean both we thank and we acknowledge. In Genesis, when Leah has her fourth son, she says, in the old Jewish translation: "This time will I praise the LORD." And she names him Yehudah, Judah. The word Jew, tradition notes, goes back to Judah. So in a sense, the very name of the people is a thank-you. On Hanukkah and Purim, a special paragraph about those miracles is added right here.
screen: `FOR OUR LIVES, IN YOUR HAND.` · `MIRACLES EVERY DAY: EVENING, MORNING, NOON.` · `NO ONE CAN THANK FOR YOU.` · `MODIM: THANK AND ACKNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `WE THANK YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow slightly in thanks. Sit or stand, and breathe. Think of three ordinary things from today: one from the morning, one from the afternoon, one from now. A cup of coffee, a message from a friend, the fact that your lungs are doing this without being asked. For each one, bow your head slightly. Just a small nod, the way you might to someone across a room. If you pray, you can say: we thank You. The bell holds the time.
Modim. We thank, we acknowledge. The Amidah's thanksgiving blessing, said with a bow, by everyone in their own words.
Your line: no one can say it for you. Today, thank one person yourself, directly, instead of letting someone else pass it on. Day five hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Jews bow at the beginning and end of Modim, the thanksgiving blessing of every Amidah; during the leader's repetition the congregation says Modim d'Rabbanan quietly, and on Hanukkah and Purim the paragraph Al hanissim is added.

fork.setup: the leader is repeating the Amidah aloud. you've answered amen to every blessing. now the leader reaches Modim. what do you do?
options: say your own quiet Modim, and bow.
fork.reveal: the congregation says Modim d'Rabbanan: someone can ask for you, but no one can thank for you.

original.note: Hebrew: we thank, we acknowledge. from y-d-h, the root of Yehudah, Judah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite thank-you near the end of a prayer.
what it means: thanks for everyday miracles, said with a bow by everyone in their own mouth.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 34a on bowing; Sotah 40a collects the rabbis' Modim texts; Genesis 29:35, Yehudah from hodaah.

sources.ref: the eighteenth blessing of the Amidah (Modim)

notes: Genesis 29:35 quoted as JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Sotah 40a: the various rabbis' versions combined into Modim d'Rabbanan; the reason 'one cannot thank through an agent' is from later commentators (e.g. Abudarham / Tur OC 127); confirm.
Modim is the eighteenth blessing in the weekday count (Retzeh seventeenth, Sim Shalom nineteenth); the outline skips Retzeh, which is mentioned in passing.
'Jew' derived from Judah / Yehudah: standard etymology.
